solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Find, perhaps, TV vets brainier somehow

indicators.note: 'somehow' means in some unspecified way, so the letters are to be arranged by whatever means works

parts.note: fourteen letters taken as printed, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Television vets turn out to be cleverer than expected, so go and find one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find' looks like an instruction to the solver, but with 'perhaps' it is an example: the word find itself is the thing being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Find needs an object (you find something), and verbs that take a direct object are called transitive by grammarians.

clue.text: Chicken and duck roll sandwiches

indicators.note: to sandwich something is to put it between two outer layers, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a roll is a list of names, as is a roster
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A deli order: chicken and duck sandwiches in a bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' and 'sandwiches' read as food, but the roll is a duty list and 'sandwiches' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male domestic fowl, one kind of chicken, so the general bird word covers it.

clue.text: Uncommercial name for mostly tinpot organisation

indicators.note: 'mostly' means most but not all, so the word loses its final letter
organisation is the act of arranging things into order, so the letters get set out afresh

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for name
taken as written
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Calling a shabby little outfit uncommercial, when really it is just second-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organisation' sits at the end as if it were the thing being described; it is the anagram signal working on name, for and most of tinpot.
explanation.definitionFit: A body that is not run to make money for owners is described as non-profit, the opposite of a commercial venture.

clue.text: Batting, have fun as a ball is being bowled

definitions.text: as a ball is being bowled

parts.note: a batsman who is batting is said to be in
to play is to have fun

explanation.surface: Advice to a cricketer: enjoy yourself out in the middle while the bowler runs in.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batting side's player at the crease is 'in'; the definition is the cricketing state of the ball while live.
explanation.definitionFit: Once the bowler begins the delivery the ball is live, and the game's term for a live ball is that phrase.

clue.text: August, time to be disrobed and showing off

indicators.note: disrobing strips away the outer clothing, so only the inside of the word stays

parts.note: the word without its outer letters
posing is showing off, putting on airs

explanation.surface: A hot August day: time to strip off and show off on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital A makes 'August' look like the month, but it is the adjective meaning grand and dignified.
explanation.definitionFit: Something august has a stately, awe-inspiring grandeur, which is the sense of the answer when used of a building or person.

clue.text: Celebrity shown up by brutal censors

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, the wrong way round
something shown is on display within the phrase, sitting in plain sight

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A famous person exposed by heavy-handed censors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shown up' reads as exposed or embarrassed; split, it signals letters on show and an upward reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat is a French borrowing meaning brilliance or renown, so it can stand for fame or celebrity.

clue.text: Foregoing a title that is meeting resistance

parts.note: an earl holds a noble title
i.e. is the abbreviation of Latin id est, that is
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Someone giving up a title because the move is meeting opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foregoing' looks like giving something up (forgoing), but here it is the adjective meaning preceding.
explanation.definitionFit: Foregoing means going before in time or order, so it is a synonym for prior or previous.

clue.text: Jokey labels stuck behind a ship when keeping watch?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: bum is British slang for the backside
a as in 'twice a day', which is per
SS stands for steamship
ticker is slang for a watch

explanation.surface: Funny slogans fixed to the stern of a vessel while someone is on watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' and 'a ship' read as nautical position; behind is the bottom (BUM), a is PER, and the ship holds a ticker.
explanation.definitionFit: Car owners glue humorous slogans to the rear fender, and the stickers are named after that part of the vehicle.

clue.text: A writer's saga: thrice a hit novel

indicators.note: novel means new and original, so the letters take on a fresh order

parts.note: fourteen letters taken as printed

explanation.surface: An author's long story became a hit three times over as a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the book the saga became, but it is the signal to rearrange the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: She was the English author of detective fiction, so she is a writer, indeed one of the best-selling ever.

clue.text: Adult party including wine periodically

indicators.note: to include is to take in as part of a whole, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a party is a group of people

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: first and third letters

explanation.surface: An adults-only party where wine is served from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests a celebration, but here it is a group of people, as in a party of walkers.
explanation.definitionFit: A fully developed person, no longer a child, is called a grown-up, the informal word for one who has reached maturity.

clue.text: Traveller turned fighter, nursing right cheek

indicators.note: something turned round faces the opposite way, so the string runs backwards
to nurse is to cradle in one's arms, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: a MiG is a Russian fighter jet
R is the abbreviation for right
lip is insolent talk, cheek

explanation.surface: A wanderer who became a soldier, tending a facial wound on the right side.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal covers everything after it: the fighter wraps right, the cheek follows, and the whole string is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilgrim journeys to a holy place, so the word is a particular kind of traveller or wayfarer.

clue.text: Tests restricting university to smaller lessons

indicators.note: to restrict is to confine within limits, so one piece is hemmed in by another

parts.note: trials are tests
U is the abbreviation for university
taken as written

explanation.surface: Exams that limit students to small-group teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like a link word joining the parts, but it is fodder, going inside the tests along with the university.
explanation.definitionFit: At British universities a tutorial is a teaching session for one student or a small group, smaller than a lecture.

clue.text: Rubbish outing ending in Crewe

parts.note: a trip is an outing

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, the only one kept here

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: A disappointing day out that finished in Crewe, a railway town in Cheshire, England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' reads as a verdict on the trip, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is cow stomach eaten as food, and by extension it is slang for worthless nonsense or drivel.

clue.text: Lacking a purpose or a meaning

parts.note: taken as written
drift is meaning, as in 'catch my drift'

explanation.surface: A shrug about life having no point or sense.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a double definition with 'or' between two meanings, but the second half is wordplay: A plus a word for meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without aim or direction in life is said to be drifting, figuratively floating loose like an untethered boat.

clue.text: Asks how to order paper?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: paper is bought by the quire, a bundle of 24 or 25 sheets

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a shopper's question; split the answer as IN QUIRES and it becomes the unit you order paper in.
explanation.definitionFit: To ask is to seek information by questioning, and the answer is the formal verb for exactly that.

clue.text: Not to be scoffed at, a French expert's clothing

indicators.note: clothing wraps round a body, so pieces wrap round another piece

parts.note: une is the French feminine for a
taken as written
able means skilled, expert

explanation.surface: A French expert's outfit is not something to mock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not to be scoffed at' is a set phrase meaning not to be sneered at; the definition stops before 'at', which is fodder. To scoff is British slang for eating greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: If food cannot be wolfed down because it is inedible, it is unfit to eat, which is the meaning of the answer.

clue.text: Following the set way for meetings to keep minutes

parts.note: pro is Latin for for, in favour of

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: fora is the Latin plural of forum, a meeting place
M is the abbreviation for minutes

explanation.surface: Following procedure, meetings should have someone taking the minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minutes' suggests the record of a meeting, but it is only the abbreviation M.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'as a matter of form', the phrase describes something done by standard procedure or a set template.

clue.text: Female assumes restraint, taking male on holiday

indicators.note: to assume a garment is to put it on, so one piece is wrapped by another

parts.note: a halter is a rope for leading an animal
F is the abbreviation for female
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A woman puts on a harness and brings a man along on a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-term is a short British school holiday in the middle of a term, usually a week.
explanation.definitionFit: Schools in Britain break for about a week midway through each term, and that break is a holiday for pupils.

clue.text: Sentry wrong to support King John at the front

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means sitting underneath, so this piece comes last
being at the front means coming first, so this piece leads its pair

parts.note: john and loo are both slang for a toilet
K is the chess abbreviation for king
out means mistaken, as in 'your sums are out'

explanation.surface: A guard wrongly backing King John, the medieval English monarch, in battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King John' reads as one historical figure, but the two words split: John is a toilet (LOO in British English) and comes before the king.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry is a soldier posted to keep watch, and a person stationed to watch for danger is called this.

clue.text: One found next to China (on northeast)

definitions.text: One found next to China (on northeast)

parts.note: NE is the compass abbreviation
china is rhyming slang for mate (china plate), so a pal
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone who lives beside China, with a note on the direction.
explanation.walkthrough: China is rhyming slang (china plate, mate); read whole, the clue also describes a native of the country bordering China, so wordplay and definition share every word.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nepali is a person from Nepal, the Himalayan country that shares a long border with China's Tibet region.

clue.text: Lover in love with Romeo, in a haze

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so a pair of pieces goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
a mist is a haze
love is zero in tennis, the letter O
Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A smitten lover and Romeo, dreamily lost in a fog of love.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo suggests Shakespeare's lover, but it gives only R, the radio code letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An amorist is a person devoted to love or lovemaking, a gallant, so it means someone who loves.

clue.text: Silent comic making you pay attention

indicators.note: something comic is absurd and topsy-turvy, so the letters are muddled up

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A mime artist whose silence makes the audience pay close attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silent comic' reads as a mime or silent-film clown; 'comic' is an adjective signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To listen is to give heed with the ears, which is what paying attention to a speaker involves.

clue.text: Bid from any, hearts, spades or clubs

indicators.note: a heart is the core of something, so only the centre letters are kept

parts.note: middle letter
middle two letters
middle letter
S is the card abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A bridge player may bid in any suit: hearts, spades or clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-table picture makes 'hearts' and 'clubs' look like suits; one selects central letters, the other means golf clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Irons are a type of golf club with a metal head, used for approach shots, so the plural fits clubs.

clue.text: Meal reduced by 1p. Great!

indicators.note: reducing something by an amount takes that amount away, so letters are removed

parts.note: supper is an evening meal
one letter P, the thing removed

explanation.surface: A shopper delighted that dinner has been discounted by a penny.
explanation.walkthrough: '1p' looks like a price (p is a British penny), but it means one letter P to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: As an exclamation of approval, super is informal for excellent, so it stands in for the cry of delight.

clue.text: Old piece of fluff among fine tufts of wool

indicators.note: to be among things is to sit in their midst, so this piece goes inside the others

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
lint is fluff from fabric
a lock is a tuft of wool or hair

explanation.surface: An old bit of fluff caught among fine woollen tufts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' reads as a bit of fluff, but it is slang for a gun; the old firearm fired by a flint striking steel.
explanation.definitionFit: Piece is slang for a gun, and the flint-sparked musket is an antique firearm, so an old gun.

clue.text: Soldier's account holding nothing back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run right to left
to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: a report is an account
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A soldier's story in which nothing is held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding nothing back' is the idiom for being frank; here it is three instructions in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private soldier in a cavalry or armoured regiment, so the word names a kind of soldier.

clue.text: Row about uniform with black beret originally and less trim

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the others

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
U is Uniform in the NATO alphabet
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: An argument over a uniform with a black beret, worn by someone who's put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with cow here, a quarrel in the surface, but the wordplay needs it to rhyme with go: a tier.
explanation.definitionFit: Trim means slim and fit, so someone less trim is plumper, and tubby is informal for short and fat.

clue.text: Diversions go into ruins to skirt labourers

parts.note: to enter is to go into

indicators.note: to skirt is to go round the edge, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: taints means spoils or ruins
men are workers, labourers

explanation.surface: Road diversions send traffic past ruins and round a gang of workmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diversions' and 'ruins' suggest roadworks and old buildings; diversions are amusements and ruins is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A diversion is something that amuses and takes the mind off things, so shows and pastimes are diversions.
